records.heading: start here
records.text: ASM BOTS is a Core War arena for 8086 assembly. You write a bot of at most 512 bytes, and the arena loads it into 64 KB of shared memory beside the other bots. It runs them one instruction at a time, and the last bot with a live process wins.

records.heading: Watch
records.text: The arena: one cell for each byte of the core, 256 bytes to a row. A bot's hue marks the bytes it wrote last; a dim cell is a zero it owns, most often a bomb. Open the arena, add two or more bots from the roster, and press fight. Each bright outline is a process, running one instruction a cycle. When a process runs a zero byte it dies, and a bot with no process left is dead. Press space to pause, . to step one cycle, and ? for every key.

records.heading: Write
records.text: The editor and the debugger: the source, its bytes, and the machine one step at a time. Open the editor and write a bot, or open one from the roster. It assembles as you type: the gutter shows each line's address and bytes, and errors and warnings mark the line and say how to fix it. test vs fights 10 rounds against a roster bot in the background and reports wins, ties, and losses. The debugger on the right steps your bot one instruction at a time, against opponents or alone.

records.heading: Compete
records.text: A bracket of eight roster bots, played in the browser: the winner of each match goes on. Tournaments run brackets, round robins, and melees of your bots and roster bots, in your browser. Every result is reproducible: a battle is a pure function of the bots, the settings, and one seed, so a share link carries the inputs, and the page that opens it plays the same battle to the same end. Hills, where your bot fights a standing field for a rank, arrive with the server.

records.heading: Write your first bot
records.text: The imp is one of the first two Core War bots (A. K. Dewdney, 1984; the dwarf is the other). It copies the instruction it runs to the next word, then runs into the copy, forever: Line by line, with the bytes each line assembles to: line bytes what it does start: call .here E8 00 00 Pushes the address of the next line, .here, and jumps there. The loader put the bot at an address you cannot know, and this is how a bot finds it. .here: pop bx 5B Takes that address into bx: the bot's start, plus 3. sub bx, .here 83 EB 03 Takes away the offset of .here (3). bx is now the bot's base, its first byte in the core. lea si, [bx+imp] 8D 77 0D si = the address of imp: where movsw copies from. lea di, [bx+imp+2] 8D 7F 0F di = one word past it: where movsw copies to. imp: movsw A5 Copies the word at si (A5 90, this line and the next) to di, and adds 2 to si and di. nop 90 Does nothing. The next instruction is at imp+2: the copy. The first five lines run once. Then the process runs the copy, which copies itself 2 bytes on, and so on around the core: one movsw and one nop for each word, so the imp moves one byte a cycle. The labels are offsets from the start of the bot, so [bx+imp] is the bot's own imp wherever it was loaded; position independence explains why that bx+ is needed. Press open in arena · vs dwarf, then fight. The dwarf drops a zero word every 4 bytes across the core, and a bomb on the word just ahead of the imp kills it. The imp writes nothing but copies of itself, so it seldom kills: over seeds 1 to 20 the dwarf wins 9 rounds, 10 last to the cycle cap and tie, and the imp wins 1, where its copies run over the dwarf's code. Try changing lea di, [bx+imp+2] to lea di, [bx+imp+4]. The copy now lands one word too far, the process runs into the zero word between, and the bot dies with dat on its 8th instruction, at cycle 7 (cycles count from 0). Step it in the debugger to watch it happen.

records.heading: What next
records.text: The machine: memory, registers, processes, death, placement, and scoring. Read it once; everything else stands on it. Language reference: every instruction, with its encoding, flags, and an example. Strategy guide, tournaments, and tools: soon. Press / to search the docs, and ? to see every key.

records.heading: One ring of 64 KB
records.text: The core is 65,536 bytes, addresses 0x0000 to 0xFFFF, and every bot shares it. There are no segments, no pages, and no protection: any process can read, write, or run any byte, its own bot's or another's. The core has no ends. One byte past 0xFFFF is 0x0000. Every address wraps. add di, 64 at di = 0xFFE0 gives 0x0020, and a write there lands at the start of the core. A word at 0xFFFF takes its high byte from 0x0000. Values wrap the same way: 16 bits for a word, 8 for a byte. Nothing faults; only running a bad instruction kills (see death).

records.heading: Empty core is DAT
records.text: At the start of a battle the core is all zeros, except the bots. The opcode 00 is dat, and a process that runs it dies. So: A jump to a random address almost always dies: most of the core is zero. A process that runs past the last instruction of its bot dies: the byte after it is zero. A bomb is a zero word, 2 bytes: mov word [di], 0 (4 bytes of code, C7 05 00 00), or stosw with ax = 0 (1 byte, AB). The arena draws empty core dark. A zero that a bot wrote is dim in that bot's hue: a bomb.

records.heading: Code is data
records.text: There is no difference between the two. The bytes of your bot are in the core with everyone else's: a bomb on your loop kills your process when it runs there, and a bot can read, copy, or change its own code as it runs. The imp copies its own instruction; a paper copies its whole body. Reads leave no trace. Only writes change the core, so a scanner can look at an enemy's code and the enemy cannot know.

records.heading: Ownership
records.text: Beside the core is an ownership map: for each byte, the bot that wrote it last. Loading a bot counts as its write, and a bomb belongs to the bot that dropped it. The arena colors the core by this map, and the bots table's footprint is the count of bytes a bot owns. Ownership has no effect on the battle. A bot can run, read, and overwrite bytes that another bot owns, and a dead bot keeps the bytes it wrote until someone writes over them.

records.heading: A lap of the ring
records.text: This bot drops a bomb every 64 bytes, starting just past its own code, for one lap of the core. The count stops the lap one bomb short of home, so it never bombs itself: di runs off the top of the core and comes back at the bottom with no code for it: the add wraps. The last bomb lands 128 bytes before end: below the bot's base, since the bot is shorter than 128 bytes. Try the stride 2: add di, 2 and mov cx, 0x10000 / 2 - 1. Now the bombs cover every second byte from end around the ring, the lap comes home, and bombs land on the bot's own loop. It dies before the lap ends. See also: the memory model in the reference, and placement for where the bots start.

records.heading: The registers
records.text: Each process has its own registers: eight 16-bit general registers, the instruction pointer, and FLAGS. The first four split into 8-bit halves. register halves in a bot ax ah al The value to store: stosw writes ax, stosb al. mul and div use it. bx bh bl The base register: by habit it holds the bot's base address, from the base idiom. cx ch cl The counter: loop and rep count it down. Shifts by cl. dx dh dl Free. mul and div use it for the high word. si The source: movs, lods, and cmps read at si. di The target: movs, stos, and scas work at di. Most bombs go through di. bp Free, and it can address memory, [bp+4]. sp The stack pointer. It starts at the bot's base, so the stack grows down into the core below the bot. ip The address of the next instruction. Only jumps, calls, ret, and loop change it by hand. FLAGS The results of the last compare or arithmetic, below. Only bx, bp, si, and di can address memory, in 8 forms: [bx+si], [bx+di], [bp+si], [bp+di], [si], [di], [bp], [bx], each with an optional constant, and [constant] alone. See ModR/M addressing.

records.heading: The start of a process
records.text: A bot's first process starts with ip and sp at the bot's base, FLAGS at 0x0002, and every other register 0. So di is 0, a fixed place in the core: a bot that bombs through di before it sets di bombs address 0, and the linter warns (uninitialized-di). A process that spl starts copies all of its parent's registers and flags, with ip at the target. Its registers are then its own: a change in one process does not reach another.

records.heading: The flags
records.text: FLAGS holds seven flags that x16c uses. The row reads, left to right, O D I T S Z A P C, as the debugger's registers panel shows it; I and T are always 0. flag name set when C carry an add carries out of the top bit, or a subtract borrows; a shift's last bit out P parity the low 8 bits of the result have an even count of 1 bits A adjust a carry or borrow crosses bit 3 Z zero the result is 0 S sign the top bit of the result is 1 D direction std sets it, cld clears it: string instructions walk down when it is set O overflow a signed result does not fit Each instruction changes its own set of flags, and the reference shows it on every entry. Two to know by heart: inc and dec leave C alone, so a loop can count with them and keep a carry. and, or, xor, and test clear C and O. mov, lea, push, pop, jumps, loop, and the string moves change no flags. Conditional jumps read the flags: jz jumps if Z is 1, jc if C is 1, jl if S and O differ. The flags reference lists each flag with what sets it and what reads it.

records.heading: D walks the string instructions
records.text: D is 0 at the start, so stosw writes at di and adds 2. After std, it takes 2 away. With rep, one instruction fills a block, one word a cycle: xor ax, ax also sets Z and clears C; nothing here reads them. The fill takes 32,512 cycles, one word each, and ends 512 bytes above the base, past the bot's code. Try deleting std. D stays 0, and di walks up instead, into the bot's own code. The tenth zero word lands on rep stosw itself, and the bot dies with dat.

records.heading: A bot is a queue of processes
records.text: A process is one thread of the bot: its registers, its flags, and its ip. A bot holds its processes in a queue, first in, first out. It starts with one process, at its base. A bot whose queue is empty is dead.

records.heading: One cycle
records.text: A battle runs in cycles. In each cycle every living bot takes one turn, and in its turn the process at the front of its queue runs one instruction. If that process is still alive, it goes to the back of the queue. A turn is one instruction of one process. A bot with 4 processes runs each of them once every 4 cycles. The bots take their turns in an order that rotates: cycle c starts with bot c mod N, where N is the count of bots loaded (dead ones included), so no bot always goes first. Every instruction costs one cycle: nop, div, and rep movsw alike. There is no timing table.

records.heading: rep: one iteration a cycle
records.text: A rep string instruction runs one iteration a cycle. After each iteration, while the repeat goes on, ip stays on the rep prefix, and the process runs it again on its next turn. So rep movsw with cx = 100 takes 100 turns, and the other bots run in between: an enemy can bomb the block while it is being copied, or bomb the rep itself and kill the process mid-copy.

records.heading: spl: more processes
records.text: spl target starts a new process at the target. The child gets a copy of the parent's registers and flags, with ip at the target, and goes into the queue just ahead of its parent. The parent goes on to the instruction after spl. With n processes, each one runs once every n turns of its bot. More processes do not make a bot faster: a bot runs one instruction a cycle whatever it holds. They make it harder to kill. A bomb kills only the process that runs it, and the bot lives while one process is left. processes a process runs to kill the bot 1 every cycle 1 bomb run 4 every 4th cycle 4 processes, each must run a bad instruction 64 every 64th cycle all 64 Processes on the same code die to the same bomb. Eight processes looping on one jmp all run into a bomb on it, one after the other. Spread them out.

records.heading: The process cap
records.text: A bot may have at most 64 processes (the arena's process cap setting). At the cap, spl does nothing: no child, no error, and the parent goes on. So a bot can split in a loop without a count.

records.heading: Four spinners
records.text: This bot starts 3 children, each on its own jmp $, and spins on a fourth: 4 processes at 4 addresses, so one bomb kills one process, not four. Six cycles in, the queue holds 4 processes: each child takes its turn before the parent reaches the next spl. From then on each process runs every 4th cycle. Load it in the debugger and step it: the processes panel shows the queue, the running process lit, a different one each cycle. Try replacing the three spl lines with spl $ + 2 three times. You get 8 processes, all on d, and one bomb on d kills them all. See also: spl in the reference, and death for what ends a process.

records.heading: death
records.text: A process dies when it runs a bad instruction. Nothing else kills it. A bot dies when its last process dies, and the battle ends when one bot or none is left.

records.heading: Every reason
records.text: The engine records a reason for each death. The arena's events log and its end table show it in their own words, with whose byte the process ran: dat · by Stone, bad opcode · self, dat · empty core. reason the arena says the process ran how it happens dat dat opcode 00 A bomb, empty core, the padding of resb, resw, and align, or the byte just past a bot's last instruction. By far the most common. undefined bad opcode a byte that is not an x16c instruction Opcodes outside the table: 0F, the segment prefixes 26 2E 36 3E, F0, INT, IN, OUT, far jumps and calls, and more; a rep prefix before anything but a string instruction; lea with a register operand; F6 /1, F7 /1, shift /6, FF /3 /5 /7. hlt hlt F4 On purpose, to end a process, or a bomb of F4 bytes. int3 int3 CC A bomb of CC bytes: 1 byte, and not zero, so a scanner that looks for code stops on it. div divide error div or idiv that fails A divisor of 0, or a quotient too large for its register: div cx with dx at or above cx, or idiv bl of -32,768 by -128.

records.heading: What does not kill
records.text: Writing anywhere. No address is protected, the bot's own code included. Reading anywhere. Reads leave no trace. Jumping anywhere. Only running the bytes there can kill. The stack. sp wraps like any address; a push past the bottom of the core writes at the top. A ret that pops garbage jumps to garbage, and the process most often dies there, not at the ret. The cycle cap. A bot alive when the battle reaches its last cycle survives, and scores.

records.heading: After death
records.text: A dead bot's bytes stay in the core, in its hue, dimmed. Its code can still run: a live process of another bot that jumps into it runs it as its own. The dead bot has no process, so it never moves again.

records.heading: One of each
records.text: Each of these bots dies at once, alone in the core, one reason each. Open one in the editor and press run until … dies in the debugger: Of the five, the linter warns only on dies-hlt (hlt-in-code), besides the missing %strategy. In the debugger, int3 in a bot's own code is a breakpoint first: the debugger stops before it, and the next step runs it. Breakpoints you set never write CC; they are checks the debugger makes, not bytes in the core. See also: dat, hlt, and int3 in the reference, and the 8086 divergences.

records.heading: Where the bots go
records.text: The loader places the bots one at a time, in the order they were entered. For each bot it draws a base address from a random number generator (PCG32) seeded with the battle's seed, and draws again until the bot keeps at least 1,024 free bytes from every bot placed before it, on both sides, around the wrap too. No enemy byte is ever within 1,024 bytes of your bot at the start. It copies the bot's bytes to the base as they are: no relocation, no fix-ups. Then the bot's first process starts at the base, with sp at the base too, so the stack grows down into the free gap below it. Each bot may draw 1,000 times; if one finds no place, the battle is invalid and does not run. That takes a crowded core: 8 bots of 512 bytes fit with ease. What this means for a bot: It cannot know where it is. It finds its base at run time, with the base idiom. It cannot know where the enemy is, only that at least 1,024 free bytes lie between them at the start. At the start, the first 1,024 bytes on either side of it hold nothing but empty core, and its own stack.

records.heading: The seed
records.text: The seed is a 32-bit number, and it is the only random thing in a battle. The same bots, in the same order, with the same settings and the same seed, give the same battle, write for write, on any machine. That is why a share link carries the seed and not a recording, and why a replay can check its own result (the verified chip). A bot that wins at one seed may lose at the next: placement decides who is close, who is aligned to whose bombs, and who is hit first. So one round proves little. The arena's seed setting is random by default, or fixed. This imp fights the dwarf at seed 1. Open it twice: the battle is the same both times, and the imp wins, as its copies run over the dwarf's code. Change the seed to 20 in the arena setup, and the dwarf wins before cycle 6,500:

records.heading: Rounds and matches
records.text: A match is K rounds. Round i (from 0) uses the seed plus i, and rotates the order of the bots by i, so each bot is placed first in turn. The match score is the sum of the rounds' points. The arena runs 1 to 10 rounds; test vs in the editor runs 10. See also: memory, and the memory model in the reference.

records.heading: Points for a round
records.text: A round is one battle. It ends when one bot or none is alive, or at the cycle cap (100,000 cycles in the arena by default). Each bot alive at the end is a survivor. With N bots in the round and S survivors, each survivor scores floor((N * N - 1) / S), and each dead bot scores 0. If every bot dies, no one scores. This is the multi-warrior scoring of pMARS, the standard Core War simulator. bots (N) 1 survivor 2 3 4 8 2 3 1 3 8 4 2 4 15 7 5 3 8 63 31 21 15 7 In a duel that is the classic 3 for a win, 1 for a tie, 0 for a loss. A bot that lives to the cycle cap is a survivor: a tie is worth points, and a bot that cannot win can still play not to lose.

records.heading: Why it is shaped this way
records.text: Each round hands out about N × N - 1 points in all, split evenly among the survivors. So a kill pays by leaving fewer bots to share with, and survival pays every round: in an 8-bot melee, one of 4 survivors scores 15, and a dead bot 0. A bot that is hard to kill scores well without killing much. The imp is the extreme case: it almost never kills, and it seldom dies.

records.heading: Points for a match
records.text: A match is K rounds with the seeds seed, seed + 1, …, seed + K - 1, and the bot order rotated each round (see placement). A bot's match score is the sum of its round points. A duel of 10 rounds with 6 wins, 3 ties, and 1 loss scores 6 × 3 + 3 × 1 = 21. The editor's test vs counts a match as wins, ties, and losses, and the arena's standings show the running points of a match of several rounds. Tournaments rank by these points too.

records.heading: A lone bot
records.text: A bot alone in the core has no one to outlive, so its battle runs until it dies or the cycle cap. That is how the debugger runs a bot with no opponents, and how you find out that it dies on its own. See also: death, for what ends a bot before the cap.

records.heading: Labels are offsets
records.text: The assembler works as if the bot starts at address 0 (org 0). A label's value is its offset from the start of the bot: in the imp, imp is 13. The loader then puts the bot at a random base and does not change a byte. So wherever a bot needs its own address in the core, it must add its base to an offset at run time.

records.heading: Relative is free
records.text: Jumps, calls, conditional jumps, loop, and spl label hold the distance to their target, not its address. Distances do not change when the bot moves, so these work wherever the bot is, with no base:

records.heading: [label] is absolute
records.text: A memory operand with no register, [label], is the ModR/M form mod 00, r/m 110: [disp16], a fixed address. It points at address label in the core: 13, say, not the bot's own byte 13, which is somewhere else. mod 00 with r/m 110 is [disp16]: an address with no register in it. The linter warns on the first line (absolute-address): "[bomb] is an absolute address: a fixed place in the core, not in this bot, which the loader places anywhere (ISA §6.4)." It proposes [bx+bomb].

records.heading: The base idiom
records.text: Every bot that touches its own bytes starts the same way: call is relative, so it works anywhere, and it pushes the address of the instruction after it, which is absolute. pop takes that address, and sub takes away its offset, 3. From then on, [bx+label] is the bot's own label, and lea di, [bx+label] puts its address in di. The idiom costs 7 bytes and 3 cycles, and uses 2 bytes of stack just under the bot. Keep bx for the base, or save it before you use bx for something else.

records.heading: Other traps
records.text: mov di, label loads the offset, 13, not an address in the bot. Use lea di, [bx+label]. $ is an offset too. jmp $ is relative and spins in place; mov ax, $ is a number, not where the bot is. Absolute jumps and splits (jmp dx, call [bx+2], spl dx) go to the address in the operand. Build it from the base first: lea dx, [bx+target]. di starts at 0. A bomb through di before di is set lands at address 0 of the core, not near the bot. The linter warns (uninitialized-di).

records.heading: A bot that reads its own data
records.text: This bot reads its bomb word through the base, then drops it every 16 bytes for one lap. The word is 0xCCCC: two int3 bytes, which kill as surely as a zero and are not zero. Try mov ax, [bomb] in place of mov ax, [bx+bomb]. The linter warns, and the bot reads address 24 of the core, not its own word. Most likely that is empty core, so it drops zero words, which kill just as well, and you might never see the bug. Unless the bot sits at address 0, the bomb it reads is not its own. See also: the memory model in the reference, and ModR/M addressing.

records.heading: the debugger tour
records.text: The debugger is the right half of the editor. It runs the same engine as the arena, on the page, so it can stop between any two cycles, show every register and byte, and go back.

records.heading: Load a bot
records.text: The debugger loads the editor's last assemble with no errors, and loads each new one by itself until you move. Alone, the bot runs until it dies or the cycle cap. To fight, add opponents from the roster next to vs in the debugger's top row, and set the seed for their placement. Once you have moved, an edit leaves the session alone and shows a source changed chip; reload loads the new text, breakpoints kept.

records.heading: The panels
records.text: panel what it shows registers The followed process's registers, ip, and FLAGS as O D I T S Z A P C toggles. A value the last step changed is lit. Click a value to edit it; Enter sets it, Esc puts it back. processes Each bot's queue, front first: ▸ marks the process that runs in the bot's next turn. Click a process to follow it: the other panels show that process. memory The core as instructions: address, bytes over a stripe in their owner's hue, label, and disassembly. It follows ip; goto takes an address, a label, or di + 4. A written byte lights up and fades. Click a row to set a breakpoint there. watch Addresses to keep an eye on, each an expression (bomb, di, bx + 0x10), read as a byte or a word. breakpoints An address or a label, with an optional condition on the registers, such as ax == 0x10 && cx < 3, and a count of its hits. trace The last 200 instructions the followed process ran. The arena strip below draws the debugger's battle with the arena's renderer. With its lock on, it stays zoomed on the followed process.

records.heading: Moving
records.text: move key what it does run, pause F5, F6, space Runs until a breakpoint, an int3 in the bot's own code, or the end of the battle. step F11, . Runs until the followed process has run one instruction. Other bots, and the bot's other processes, run their turns in between. step over F10 A step, except that a call runs until it returns, and a rep until it is done. step out shift+F11 Runs until the process returns from the current call. run to cursor Runs until a process is about to run the editor cursor's line. run until … dies Runs until the followed process's bot has no process left. run N cycles Runs the count of cycles in the field beside it. step back , Goes back one step, or one cycle of a run: 256 deep. reset Starts the battle again from cycle 0, breakpoints kept. breakpoint F9 Sets or clears a breakpoint on the cursor's line. speed [ ] Slower or faster runs. 0 shows the whole core in the strip. The function keys work with the focus anywhere, the editor included. Press ? for every key of the page. Breakpoints are checks the debugger makes before each cycle, never CC bytes in the core, so a breakpoint cannot change the battle. An int3 in the bot's own code is a stop too: the debugger halts before it, and the next move runs it, and the process dies as it would in the arena.

records.heading: Walk through the imp
records.text: Open this block in the editor, then step it with F11 and watch the registers: call .here: sp drops by 2, from the base. In memory, the 2 bytes under the base light up: the address of .here, base + 3. pop bx: bx is base + 3, and sp is back at the base. sub bx, .here: bx is the base. Compare it with the base the processes panel shows. lea si, [bx+imp] and lea di, [bx+imp+2]: si and di are 2 apart, 13 and 15 bytes past the base. movsw: the 2 bytes at di light up in memory, A5 90, and si and di each grow by 2. nop, and ip is on the copy. Press F5: the imp walks. Then add the dwarf next to vs, press run until Imp dies, and step back from the end to see the bomb that killed it. Not every seed has one: at some the imp lives to the cycle cap. See also: processes and cycles, for what a step runs, and death, for what ends one.

records.heading: data movement
records.text: These instructions move bytes and words between registers, memory, and the stack. None changes a flag, except popf and sahf, which load them. Every write to memory marks the bytes as the writer's in the ownership map. On this page: mov · lea · xchg · push · pop · pushf · popf · sahf · lahf · cbw · cwd.

records.heading: mov
records.text: Copy a byte or word: dst = src. form encoding example bytes mov r/m8, r8 88 /r mov [bx+4], dl 88 57 04 mov r/m16, r16 89 /r mov [di], dx 89 15 mov r8, r/m8 8A /r mov dl, [bx+4] 8A 57 04 mov r16, r/m16 8B /r mov dx, [di] 8B 15 mov al, [moffs16] A0 iw mov al, [0x0100] A0 00 01 mov ax, [moffs16] A1 iw mov ax, [0x0100] A1 00 01 mov [moffs16], al A2 iw mov [0x0100], al A2 00 01 mov [moffs16], ax A3 iw mov [0x0100], ax A3 00 01 mov r8, imm8 B0+r ib mov bl, 0x41 B3 41 mov r16, imm16 B8+r iw mov si, 0x1234 BE 34 12 mov r/m8, imm8 C6 /0 ib mov byte [bx+4], 0x41 C6 47 04 41 mov r/m16, imm16 C7 /0 iw mov word [di], 0x1234 C7 05 34 12 Flags: none change. Cycles: 1. In a bot: Writes bombs and reads data. mov word [di], 0 is the dwarf's bomb: two zero bytes, one DAT. Idiom: mov ax, [label] reads the fixed address label of the core, not your copy of it: the loader does not relocate. Read your own data as [bx+label] after the base idiom. See also: lea · xchg · stosw

records.heading: lea
records.text: Load the address of a memory operand, not the value there. form encoding example bytes lea r16, m 8D /r lea dx, [bx+di-2] 8D 51 FE Flags: none change. Cycles: 1. In a bot: Computes an address from a base register, with no memory access: lea di, [bx+end] points di just past the bot. Idiom: lea takes a memory operand only: lea ax, bx is an error, and the bytes 8D with mod = 11 kill. It changes no flags, so it cannot stand in for add before a jz. See also: mov · add

records.heading: xchg
records.text: Swap the two operands. form encoding example bytes xchg r/m8, r8 86 /r xchg [bx+4], dl 86 57 04 xchg r/m16, r16 87 /r xchg [di], dx 87 15 xchg ax, r16 90+r xchg ax, si 96 Flags: none change. Cycles: 1. In a bot: Swaps two values in one instruction, with no scratch register. Paper swaps the bytes of its base to start its path far away. Idiom: xchg with a memory operand writes that memory: xchg ax, [si] to read a word also stores ax there. xchg ax, ax assembles to 87 C0, because 90 is nop. See also: mov · push · nop

records.heading: push
records.text: Sp -= 2, then store the word at sp. form encoding example bytes push r16 50+r push si 56 push r/m16 FF /6 push word [di] FF 35 Flags: none change. Cycles: 1. In a bot: Writes a word at sp - 2 and moves sp down: a store and a step in 1 byte. sp starts at the base, so the stack grows into the core under the bot. Idiom: push sp pushes sp after the decrement, as the 8086 does. push 5 is an error: the 8086 has no push imm. Load a register first. See also: pop · call · pushf

records.heading: pop
records.text: Load the word at sp into dst, then sp += 2. form encoding example bytes pop r16 58+r pop si 5E pop r/m16 8F /0 pop word [di] 8F 05 Flags: none change. Cycles: 1. In a bot: Reads the word at sp and moves sp up. After call, it gets the address of the next line: the base idiom. Idiom: The word at sp is whatever the core holds there, enemy bombs included. pop sp leaves sp equal to the popped word, not that word plus 2. See also: push · call · ret

records.heading: pushf
records.text: Push FLAGS. form encoding example bytes pushf 9C pushf 9C Flags: none change. Cycles: 1. In a bot: Saves the flags across code that changes them. Idiom: It writes 2 bytes at sp - 2 like any push: with sp at the base, the word just under the bot. Bit 1 of the word is 1, and I and T are 0. See also: popf · lahf · push

records.heading: popf
records.text: Pop a word into FLAGS: OF DF SF ZF AF PF CF. form encoding example bytes popf 9D popf 9D Cycles: 1. In a bot: Puts back flags that pushf saved, or sets several flags from a word. Idiom: Only OF DF SF ZF AF PF CF take bits from the word; the others are lost. A stray word on the stack can set DF, and then every string instruction runs backward. See also: pushf · sahf · std

records.heading: sahf
records.text: Copy ah into SF ZF AF PF CF. form encoding example bytes sahf 9E sahf 9E Cycles: 1. In a bot: Sets SF ZF AF PF CF from ah in one byte. Idiom: It does not touch OF or DF. The bits of ah are SF ZF - AF - PF - CF from bit 7 down, so ZF is bit 6, not bit 0. See also: lahf · popf

records.heading: lahf
records.text: Copy SF ZF AF PF CF into ah. form encoding example bytes lahf 9F lahf 9F Flags: none change. Cycles: 1. In a bot: Copies SF ZF AF PF CF into ah, so a flag becomes a value to test, store, or add. Idiom: Bits 5, 3, and 1 of ah are 0, 0, and 1, not flags. OF is not in ah: use pushf for it. See also: sahf · pushf

records.heading: cbw
records.text: Sign-extend al into ax. form encoding example bytes cbw 98 cbw 98 Flags: none change. Cycles: 1. In a bot: Widens a signed byte to a word before word math: al = -8 becomes ax = -8. Idiom: It overwrites ah. For an unsigned byte, clear ah instead (mov ah, 0): cbw turns 0x80..0xFF into 0xFF80..0xFFFF. See also: cwd · lodsb

records.heading: cwd
records.text: Sign-extend ax into dx:ax. form encoding example bytes cwd 99 cwd 99 Flags: none change. Cycles: 1. In a bot: Sets dx to the sign of ax before a signed divide. Idiom: Before an unsigned div, clear dx with xor dx, dx: when ax is 0x8000 or more, cwd sets dx to 0xFFFF, the quotient does not fit, and the divide kills. See also: cbw · div · idiv

records.heading: arithmetic
records.text: Integer math on bytes and words. Every result wraps: a word to 16 bits, a byte to 8. add, adc, sub, sbb, cmp, and neg set all six status flags; inc and dec set all but CF. div and idiv kill the process on a 0 divisor or a quotient that does not fit. add byte [mem], reg does not exist here: its opcode, 00, is DAT (see 8086 divergences). On this page: add · adc · sub · sbb · cmp · neg · mul · imul · div · idiv · inc · dec.

records.heading: add
records.text: Add: dst += src. form encoding example bytes add r/m16, r16 01 /r add [di], dx 01 15 add r8, r/m8 02 /r add dl, [bx+4] 02 57 04 add r16, r/m16 03 /r add dx, [di] 03 15 add al, imm8 04 ib add al, 0x41 04 41 add ax, imm16 05 iw add ax, 0x1234 05 34 12 add r/m8, imm8 80 /0 ib add byte [bx+4], 0x41 80 47 04 41 add r/m16, imm16 81 /0 iw add word [di], 0x1234 81 05 34 12 add r/m16, imm8 83 /0 ib add word [di], 4 83 05 04 Cycles: 1. In a bot: Steps a pointer by the stride: the heart of every bomber loop. Idiom: add byte [bx], al is an error: its opcode 00 is DAT (ISA §9). Use a word add or add byte [bx], imm8. A byte add of two registers works: it uses 02 /r. See also: adc · sub · inc

records.heading: adc
records.text: Add with carry: dst += src + CF, to chain adds past 16 bits. form encoding example bytes adc r/m8, r8 10 /r adc [bx+4], dl 10 57 04 adc r/m16, r16 11 /r adc [di], dx 11 15 adc r8, r/m8 12 /r adc dl, [bx+4] 12 57 04 adc r16, r/m16 13 /r adc dx, [di] 13 15 adc al, imm8 14 ib adc al, 0x41 14 41 adc ax, imm16 15 iw adc ax, 0x1234 15 34 12 adc r/m8, imm8 80 /2 ib adc byte [bx+4], 0x41 80 57 04 41 adc r/m16, imm16 81 /2 iw adc word [di], 0x1234 81 15 34 12 adc r/m16, imm8 83 /2 ib adc word [di], 4 83 15 04 Cycles: 1. In a bot: Carries a 16-bit add into a second word: 32-bit counters and random-number math. Idiom: It adds CF, whatever set it. At the start of a chain, use add, or clear CF with clc first. See also: add · sbb · clc

records.heading: sub
records.text: Subtract: dst -= src. form encoding example bytes sub r/m8, r8 28 /r sub [bx+4], dl 28 57 04 sub r/m16, r16 29 /r sub [di], dx 29 15 sub r8, r/m8 2A /r sub dl, [bx+4] 2A 57 04 sub r16, r/m16 2B /r sub dx, [di] 2B 15 sub al, imm8 2C ib sub al, 0x41 2C 41 sub ax, imm16 2D iw sub ax, 0x1234 2D 34 12 sub r/m8, imm8 80 /5 ib sub byte [bx+4], 0x41 80 6F 04 41 sub r/m16, imm16 81 /5 iw sub word [di], 0x1234 81 2D 34 12 sub r/m16, imm8 83 /5 ib sub word [di], 4 83 2D 04 Cycles: 1. In a bot: Steps down, and turns an address into a distance: sub bx, .here in the base idiom, and sub dx, bx to find a hit relative to the base. Idiom: sub changes CF and dec does not. A distance under the base wraps to a large number: that is why one unsigned cmp checks both ends of a range. See also: sbb · cmp · neg · dec

records.heading: sbb
records.text: Subtract with borrow: dst -= src + CF, to chain subtracts past 16 bits. form encoding example bytes sbb r/m8, r8 18 /r sbb [bx+4], dl 18 57 04 sbb r/m16, r16 19 /r sbb [di], dx 19 15 sbb r8, r/m8 1A /r sbb dl, [bx+4] 1A 57 04 sbb r16, r/m16 1B /r sbb dx, [di] 1B 15 sbb al, imm8 1C ib sbb al, 0x41 1C 41 sbb ax, imm16 1D iw sbb ax, 0x1234 1D 34 12 sbb r/m8, imm8 80 /3 ib sbb byte [bx+4], 0x41 80 5F 04 41 sbb r/m16, imm16 81 /3 iw sbb word [di], 0x1234 81 1D 34 12 sbb r/m16, imm8 83 /3 ib sbb word [di], 4 83 1D 04 Cycles: 1. In a bot: Subtracts past 16 bits, and turns CF into a mask: sbb ax, ax is 0 or 0xFFFF. Idiom: It subtracts CF as well. After cmp or sub, CF is a borrow; clear it with clc when the chain starts fresh. See also: sub · adc · cmc

records.heading: cmp
records.text: Compare: set the flags from dst - src; dst keeps its value. form encoding example bytes cmp r/m8, r8 38 /r cmp [bx+4], dl 38 57 04 cmp r/m16, r16 39 /r cmp [di], dx 39 15 cmp r8, r/m8 3A /r cmp dl, [bx+4] 3A 57 04 cmp r16, r/m16 3B /r cmp dx, [di] 3B 15 cmp al, imm8 3C ib cmp al, 0x41 3C 41 cmp ax, imm16 3D iw cmp ax, 0x1234 3D 34 12 cmp r/m8, imm8 80 /7 ib cmp byte [bx+4], 0x41 80 7F 04 41 cmp r/m16, imm16 81 /7 iw cmp word [di], 0x1234 81 3D 34 12 cmp r/m16, imm8 83 /7 ib cmp word [di], 4 83 3D 04 Cycles: 1. In a bot: Tests a value and keeps it: the scanner's cmp word [si], 0 asks if a word is empty core. Idiom: The jump after it picks signed or unsigned: jb and ja compare unsigned, jl and jg compare signed. Addresses are unsigned. See also: sub · test · jz · ja · jl

records.heading: neg
records.text: Negate: dst = 0 - dst. form encoding example bytes neg r/m8 F6 /3 neg byte [bx+4] F6 5F 04 neg r/m16 F7 /3 neg word [di] F7 1D Cycles: 1. In a bot: Turns a stride around, or a negative distance into a positive one. Idiom: CF is 1 for every value but 0. neg of 0x8000 is 0x8000, with OF set. See also: not · sub

records.heading: mul
records.text: Unsigned multiply: ax = al * src (word: dx:ax = ax * src). form encoding example bytes mul r/m8 F6 /4 mul byte [bx+4] F6 67 04 mul r/m16 F7 /4 mul word [di] F7 25 Cycles: 1. In a bot: Multiplies for a random walk: one step of a linear congruential generator (LCG). Idiom: It writes dx (ah for a byte) even when the product is small. It takes no immediate: mul 5 is an error. See also: imul · div · shl

records.heading: imul
records.text: Signed multiply: ax = al * src (word: dx:ax = ax * src). form encoding example bytes imul r/m8 F6 /5 imul byte [bx+4] F6 6F 04 imul r/m16 F7 /5 imul word [di] F7 2D Cycles: 1. In a bot: Multiplies signed values, for strides that can be negative. Idiom: Only the 1-operand form exists: imul ax, bx, 3 (80186) is an error. ZF SF AF PF read 0 after it, so jz does not test the product. See also: mul · idiv · cwd

records.heading: div
records.text: Unsigned divide ax (word: dx:ax) by src; a 0 divisor or an overflow kills. form encoding example bytes div r/m8 F6 /6 div byte [bx+4] F6 77 04 div r/m16 F7 /6 div word [di] F7 35 Flags: none change. Cycles: 1. A 0 divisor, or a quotient that does not fit, kills the process with reason div. In a bot: Divides unsigned: the remainder wraps a counter into a range. Idiom: A 0 divisor, or a quotient too big for ax (al for a byte), kills the process with reason div. dx is the high half of the dividend: clear it first. See also: idiv · mul · cwd

records.heading: idiv
records.text: Signed divide ax (word: dx:ax) by src; a 0 divisor or an overflow kills. form encoding example bytes idiv r/m8 F6 /7 idiv byte [bx+4] F6 7F 04 idiv r/m16 F7 /7 idiv word [di] F7 3D Flags: none change. Cycles: 1. A 0 divisor, or a quotient that does not fit, kills the process with reason div. In a bot: Divides signed; the quotient rounds toward 0. Idiom: It kills on a 0 divisor, on a quotient out of range, and on a quotient of exactly -32768 (-128 for a byte), as the 8086 does. See also: div · cwd · cbw

records.heading: inc
records.text: Add 1; CF keeps its value. form encoding example bytes inc r16 40+r inc si 46 inc r/m8 FE /0 inc byte [bx+4] FE 47 04 inc r/m16 FF /0 inc word [di] FF 05 Cycles: 1. In a bot: Counts up. inc r16 is 1 byte (40+r); add r16, 1 is 3. Idiom: It keeps CF, so a jc after it reads an older carry. At 0xFFFF it wraps to 0 and sets ZF. See also: dec · add

records.heading: dec
records.text: Subtract 1; CF keeps its value. form encoding example bytes dec r16 48+r dec si 4E dec r/m8 FE /1 dec byte [bx+4] FE 4F 04 dec r/m16 FF /1 dec word [di] FF 0D Cycles: 1. In a bot: Counts down. dec word [x] in a tight loop is an imp gate: the word changes every turn, so an imp that lands on it breaks. Idiom: It keeps CF, like inc. For a counted loop, loop does the dec cx and the jump in one instruction and keeps the flags. See also: inc · loop · sub

records.heading: logic
records.text: Bitwise operations on bytes and words. and, or, xor, and test set CF, OF, and AF to 0 and ZF, SF, and PF from the result. not changes no flag. On this page: and · or · xor · not · test.

records.heading: and
records.text: Bitwise and: dst &= src; clears CF and OF. form encoding example bytes and r/m8, r8 20 /r and [bx+4], dl 20 57 04 and r/m16, r16 21 /r and [di], dx 21 15 and r8, r/m8 22 /r and dl, [bx+4] 22 57 04 and r16, r/m16 23 /r and dx, [di] 23 15 and al, imm8 24 ib and al, 0x41 24 41 and ax, imm16 25 iw and ax, 0x1234 25 34 12 and r/m8, imm8 80 /4 ib and byte [bx+4], 0x41 80 67 04 41 and r/m16, imm16 81 /4 iw and word [di], 0x1234 81 25 34 12 and r/m16, imm8 83 /4 ib and word [di], 4 83 25 04 Cycles: 1. In a bot: Masks: keeps a pointer inside a window, or picks bits out. Idiom: The mask wraps a counter only when it is a power of 2 minus 1. and sets CF and OF to 0. See also: or · test · xor

records.heading: or
records.text: Bitwise or: dst |= src; clears CF and OF. form encoding example bytes or r/m8, r8 08 /r or [bx+4], dl 08 57 04 or r/m16, r16 09 /r or [di], dx 09 15 or r8, r/m8 0A /r or dl, [bx+4] 0A 57 04 or r16, r/m16 0B /r or dx, [di] 0B 15 or al, imm8 0C ib or al, 0x41 0C 41 or ax, imm16 0D iw or ax, 0x1234 0D 34 12 or r/m8, imm8 80 /1 ib or byte [bx+4], 0x41 80 4F 04 41 or r/m16, imm16 81 /1 iw or word [di], 0x1234 81 0D 34 12 or r/m16, imm8 83 /1 ib or word [di], 4 83 0D 04 Cycles: 1. In a bot: Merges values. A chain of or tests several words for non-zero in one jump, as the vampire samples the core. Idiom: or ax, ax sets the flags like test ax, ax but writes ax back. With a memory destination, that is a write to the core. See also: and · xor · test

records.heading: xor
records.text: Bitwise xor: dst ^= src; clears CF and OF. form encoding example bytes xor r/m8, r8 30 /r xor [bx+4], dl 30 57 04 xor r/m16, r16 31 /r xor [di], dx 31 15 xor r8, r/m8 32 /r xor dl, [bx+4] 32 57 04 xor r16, r/m16 33 /r xor dx, [di] 33 15 xor al, imm8 34 ib xor al, 0x41 34 41 xor ax, imm16 35 iw xor ax, 0x1234 35 34 12 xor r/m8, imm8 80 /6 ib xor byte [bx+4], 0x41 80 77 04 41 xor r/m16, imm16 81 /6 iw xor word [di], 0x1234 81 35 34 12 xor r/m16, imm8 83 /6 ib xor word [di], 4 83 35 04 Cycles: 1. In a bot: xor ax, ax zeros a register in 2 bytes: the usual bomb value. Idiom: xor ax, ax also sets ZF and clears CF; mov ax, 0 keeps the flags. Between a cmp and its jump, use mov. See also: and · or · not · mov

records.heading: not
records.text: Flip every bit of dst. form encoding example bytes not r/m8 F6 /2 not byte [bx+4] F6 57 04 not r/m16 F7 /2 not word [di] F7 15 Flags: none change. Cycles: 1. In a bot: Flips every bit: 0 becomes 0xFFFF, a non-zero fill. Idiom: It changes no flag: a jz after not reads the flags from before. not is one less than neg: not x = -x - 1. See also: neg · xor

records.heading: test
records.text: And without storing: set the flags from dst & src. form encoding example bytes test r/m8, r8 84 /r test [bx+4], dl 84 57 04 test r/m16, r16 85 /r test [di], dx 85 15 test al, imm8 A8 ib test al, 0x41 A8 41 test ax, imm16 A9 iw test ax, 0x1234 A9 34 12 test r/m8, imm8 F6 /0 ib test byte [bx+4], 0x41 F6 47 04 41 test r/m16, imm16 F7 /0 iw test word [di], 0x1234 F7 05 34 12 Cycles: 1. In a bot: Checks bits and writes nothing: test ax, ax then jz asks if ax is 0. Idiom: test al, 1 then jz jumps when the bit is 0, not when it is 1. It sets CF and OF to 0. See also: and · cmp · jz

records.heading: shifts and rotates
records.text: Shifts and rotates by 1 or by cl, the only counts the 8086 takes. The count is not masked: a count of 40 in cl shifts 40 times, in one cycle like any instruction. Shifts set ZF, SF, and PF from the result; rotates change only CF and OF. A count of 0 changes no flag. On this page: rol · ror · rcl · rcr · shl · shr · sar.

records.heading: rol
records.text: Rotate left: the top bit goes to bit 0 and CF. form encoding example bytes rol r/m8, 1 D0 /0 rol byte [bx+4], 1 D0 47 04 rol r/m16, 1 D1 /0 rol word [di], 1 D1 05 rol r/m8, cl D2 /0 rol byte [bx+4], cl D2 47 04 rol r/m16, cl D3 /0 rol word [di], cl D3 05 Cycles: 1. In a bot: Rotates bits around with none lost: a stride that changes each pass and never becomes 0. Idiom: The count is 1 or cl, and a count in cl is not masked: a word rotate by 17 is a rotate by 1, 17 steps. A count of 0 changes no flag. See also: ror · rcl · shl

records.heading: ror
records.text: Rotate right: bit 0 goes to the top bit and CF. form encoding example bytes ror r/m8, 1 D0 /1 ror byte [bx+4], 1 D0 4F 04 ror r/m16, 1 D1 /1 ror word [di], 1 D1 0D ror r/m8, cl D2 /1 ror byte [bx+4], cl D2 4F 04 ror r/m16, cl D3 /1 ror word [di], cl D3 0D Cycles: 1. In a bot: Rotates right. A word rotate by 8 swaps its bytes. Idiom: Only 1 and cl are counts: ror ax, 8 is an error on the 8086. xchg al, ah is shorter. See also: rol · rcr · xchg

records.heading: rcl
records.text: Rotate left through CF. form encoding example bytes rcl r/m8, 1 D0 /2 rcl byte [bx+4], 1 D0 57 04 rcl r/m16, 1 D1 /2 rcl word [di], 1 D1 15 rcl r/m8, cl D2 /2 rcl byte [bx+4], cl D2 57 04 rcl r/m16, cl D3 /2 rcl word [di], cl D3 15 Cycles: 1. In a bot: Shifts CF into bit 0: carries a shift into a second word, or turns a flag into a bit. Idiom: It reads CF: a stale carry goes into bit 0. Use clc first when it must be 0. See also: rcr · rol · clc

records.heading: rcr
records.text: Rotate right through CF. form encoding example bytes rcr r/m8, 1 D0 /3 rcr byte [bx+4], 1 D0 5F 04 rcr r/m16, 1 D1 /3 rcr word [di], 1 D1 1D rcr r/m8, cl D2 /3 rcr byte [bx+4], cl D2 5F 04 rcr r/m16, cl D3 /3 rcr word [di], cl D3 1D Cycles: 1. In a bot: Shifts CF into the top bit: the low word of a 32-bit right shift. Idiom: It reads CF into bit 15. After shr dx, 1, CF is the bit that fell out of dx, which is what a 32-bit shift needs. See also: rcl · shr · stc

records.heading: shl
records.text: Shift left, zeros in: an unsigned double. Also written sal. form encoding example bytes shl r/m8, 1 D0 /4 shl byte [bx+4], 1 D0 67 04 shl r/m16, 1 D1 /4 shl word [di], 1 D1 25 shl r/m8, cl D2 /4 shl byte [bx+4], cl D2 67 04 shl r/m16, cl D3 /4 shl word [di], cl D3 25 Cycles: 1. In a bot: Doubles: shl ax, 1 is ax * 2 in one cycle, with no mul. Idiom: sal is the same instruction. Bits shifted past bit 15 are gone; CF holds the last one out. See also: shr · sar · mul

records.heading: shr
records.text: Shift right, zeros in: an unsigned halve. form encoding example bytes shr r/m8, 1 D0 /5 shr byte [bx+4], 1 D0 6F 04 shr r/m16, 1 D1 /5 shr word [di], 1 D1 2D shr r/m8, cl D2 /5 shr byte [bx+4], cl D2 6F 04 shr r/m16, cl D3 /5 shr word [di], cl D3 2D Cycles: 1. In a bot: Halves unsigned: bytes to words for a copy, or a step of a binary search. Idiom: An odd value loses its low bit. To round a byte count up to words, add 1 first: (SIZE + 1) / 2. See also: shl · sar · rcr

records.heading: sar
records.text: Shift right, copies of the sign bit in: a signed halve. form encoding example bytes sar r/m8, 1 D0 /7 sar byte [bx+4], 1 D0 7F 04 sar r/m16, 1 D1 /7 sar word [di], 1 D1 3D sar r/m8, cl D2 /7 sar byte [bx+4], cl D2 7F 04 sar r/m16, cl D3 /7 sar word [di], cl D3 3D Cycles: 1. In a bot: Halves signed: the sign bit stays. Idiom: It rounds toward minus infinity, where idiv by 2 rounds toward 0. -1 stays -1 however far it shifts. See also: shr · idiv

records.heading: control flow
records.text: jmp, call, loop, and the conditional jumps take a target relative to the next instruction, so they work wherever the loader puts the bot. jmp and call with a register or memory operand go to the absolute address it holds. The conditional jumps, the loop forms, and jcxz are rel8 only: -128..+127 bytes from the next instruction. The assembler does not stretch them; a target out of reach is the error jump-out-of-range. For a far target, invert the condition and jump over a jmp: On this page: jmp · call · ret · jo · jno · jc · jnc · jz · jnz · jna · ja · js · jns · jpe · jpo · jl · jnl · jng · jg · loopne · loope · loop · jcxz.

records.heading: Conditions
records.text: What each jump tests, and what it means after cmp a, b: jump also written jumps when after cmp a, b jo OF = 1 signed overflow jno OF = 0 no signed overflow jc jb, jnae CF = 1 a < b, unsigned jnc jae, jnb CF = 0 a >= b, unsigned jz je ZF = 1 a = b jnz jne ZF = 0 a ≠ b jna jbe CF = 1 or ZF = 1 a <= b, unsigned ja jnbe CF = 0 and ZF = 0 a > b, unsigned js SF = 1 a - b is negative jns SF = 0 a - b is 0 or positive jpe jp PF = 1 the low byte of a - b has an even count of 1 bits jpo jnp PF = 0 the low byte of a - b has an odd count of 1 bits jl jnge SF ≠ OF a < b, signed jnl jge SF = OF a >= b, signed jng jle ZF = 1 or SF ≠ OF a <= b, signed jg jnle ZF = 0 and SF = OF a > b, signed loopne loopnz cx ≠ 0 and ZF = 0, after cx -= 1 (a counted search) loope loopz cx ≠ 0 and ZF = 1, after cx -= 1 (a counted skip) loop cx ≠ 0, after cx -= 1 (a counted loop) jcxz cx = 0 (a loop guard)

records.heading: jmp
records.text: Jump to a label, or to the address in a register or memory. form encoding example bytes jmp rel8 EB cb jmp $+0x10 EB 0E jmp rel16 E9 cw jmp $+0x300 E9 FD 02 jmp r/m16 FF /4 jmp dx FF E2 Flags: none change. Cycles: 1. In a bot: Loops and skips data. jmp $ spins in place: a process that stays alive and does nothing. Idiom: jmp label is relative and position independent; jmp bx and jmp word [x] go to an absolute address. There is no conditional rel16 jump: to reach far, jump over a jmp with the inverted condition. See also: call · jz · spl

records.heading: call
records.text: Push the address of the next instruction, then jump. form encoding example bytes call rel16 E8 cw call $+0x300 E8 FD 02 call r/m16 FF /2 call dx FF D2 Flags: none change. Cycles: 1. In a bot: Mostly the base idiom: call .here pushes the address of .here, and pop bx takes it. Idiom: call writes the return address at sp - 2: with sp at the base, the 2 bytes just under the bot. A bomb there turns the ret into a jump to 0. See also: ret · pop · push

records.heading: ret
records.text: Pop an address and jump to it; ret n then drops n more bytes. form encoding example bytes ret C3 ret C3 ret imm16 C2 iw ret 2 C2 02 00 Flags: none change. Cycles: 1. In a bot: Returns from a call, or jumps to any address on the stack: push dx then ret is jmp dx. Idiom: It trusts the stack: the word at sp may be anything. ret n pops, then adds n to sp. See also: call · jmp · pop

records.heading: jo
records.text: Jump if overflow: OF=1. form encoding example bytes jo rel8 70 cb jo $+0x10 70 0E Flags: none change. Cycles: 1. In a bot: Catches a signed overflow, to clamp a value. Rare in bots. Idiom: OF is signed overflow; for an unsigned one, test CF with jc. See also: jno · jc

records.heading: jno
records.text: Jump if no overflow: OF=0. form encoding example bytes jno rel8 71 cb jno $+0x10 71 0E Flags: none change. Cycles: 1. In a bot: Goes on while a signed value has not wrapped. Idiom: inc and dec set OF too: 0x7FFF + 1 overflows. See also: jo · jnc

records.heading: jc
records.text: Jump if carry, or below unsigned: CF=1. Also written jb, jnae. form encoding example bytes jc rel8 72 cb jc $+0x10 72 0E Flags: none change. Cycles: 1. In a bot: Unsigned below: after cmp a, b, jumps if a < b. It also reads the bit a shift pushed out. Idiom: jb, jc, and jnae are one instruction. inc and dec keep CF, so a jc after them reads an older carry. See also: jnc · cmp · stc

records.heading: jnc
records.text: Jump if no carry, or above or equal unsigned: CF=0. Also written jae, jnb. form encoding example bytes jnc rel8 73 cb jnc $+0x10 73 0E Flags: none change. Cycles: 1. In a bot: Unsigned above or equal: after cmp a, b, jumps if a >= b. Idiom: jae, jnb, and jnc are one instruction. It is unsigned: -1 (0xFFFF) is above everything. See also: jc · ja

records.heading: jz
records.text: Jump if zero, or equal: ZF=1. Also written je. form encoding example bytes jz rel8 74 cb jz $+0x10 74 0E Flags: none change. Cycles: 1. In a bot: Equal, or zero: after cmp, after test, or after a count reaches 0. Idiom: je and jz are one instruction. rel8 only: the target must be within -128..+127 bytes. See also: jnz · cmp · test

records.heading: jnz
records.text: Jump if not zero, or not equal: ZF=0. Also written jne. form encoding example bytes jnz rel8 75 cb jnz $+0x10 75 0E Flags: none change. Cycles: 1. In a bot: Loops until a count reaches 0, or jumps on not equal. Idiom: loop does dec cx and the jump in one instruction; dec and jnz work with any register. See also: jz · loop · dec

records.heading: jna
records.text: Jump if not above, unsigned: CF=1 or ZF=1. Also written jbe. form encoding example bytes jna rel8 76 cb jna $+0x10 76 0E Flags: none change. Cycles: 1. In a bot: Unsigned below or equal: one compare checks that a value is in 0..n. Idiom: It is unsigned: -1 (0xFFFF) is above 63. That is what makes one cmp a range check. See also: ja · jc · cmp

records.heading: ja
records.text: Jump if above, unsigned: CF=0 and ZF=0. Also written jnbe. form encoding example bytes ja rel8 77 cb ja $+0x10 77 0E Flags: none change. Cycles: 1. In a bot: Unsigned above: after cmp a, b, jumps if a > b. Idiom: ja is unsigned; jg is its signed twin. For addresses, use ja. See also: jna · jg · cmp

records.heading: js
records.text: Jump if sign, negative: SF=1. form encoding example bytes js rel8 78 cb js $+0x10 78 0E Flags: none change. Cycles: 1. In a bot: Negative: bit 15 of the result is 1. Idiom: After a signed overflow, SF is wrong; jl reads SF and OF together and is right. See also: jns · jl

records.heading: jns
records.text: Jump if not sign, 0 or positive: SF=0. form encoding example bytes jns rel8 79 cb jns $+0x10 79 0E Flags: none change. Cycles: 1. In a bot: Zero or positive: bit 15 of the result is 0. Idiom: Addresses 0x8000 and up read as negative: do not use jns to compare addresses. See also: js · jnl

records.heading: jpe
records.text: Jump if parity even, an even count of 1 bits in the low byte: PF=1. Also written jp. form encoding example bytes jpe rel8 7A cb jpe $+0x10 7A 0E Flags: none change. Cycles: 1. In a bot: Parity of the low byte: an even count of 1 bits. Rare in bots. Idiom: PF counts the low 8 bits only, even for a word result. See also: jpo · test

records.heading: jpo
records.text: Jump if parity odd, an odd count of 1 bits in the low byte: PF=0. Also written jnp. form encoding example bytes jpo rel8 7B cb jpo $+0x10 7B 0E Flags: none change. Cycles: 1. In a bot: Parity of the low byte: an odd count of 1 bits. Idiom: jnp and jpo are one instruction. PF counts the low 8 bits only. See also: jpe · and

records.heading: jl
records.text: Jump if less, signed: SF≠OF. Also written jnge. form encoding example bytes jl rel8 7C cb jl $+0x10 7C 0E Flags: none change. Cycles: 1. In a bot: Signed less: after cmp a, b, jumps if a < b as signed values. Idiom: It is signed: 0xFFFF is -1, less than 0. For addresses, use jb. See also: jnl · jc · cmp

records.heading: jnl
records.text: Jump if not less, signed: SF=OF. Also written jge. form encoding example bytes jnl rel8 7D cb jnl $+0x10 7D 0E Flags: none change. Cycles: 1. In a bot: Signed greater or equal. After sub ax, n, it tests the old ax against n. Idiom: jge and jnl are one instruction. It reads SF and OF, not CF. See also: jl · jng · jnc

records.heading: jng
records.text: Jump if not greater, signed: ZF=1 or SF≠OF. Also written jle. form encoding example bytes jng rel8 7E cb jng $+0x10 7E 0E Flags: none change. Cycles: 1. In a bot: Signed less or equal: guards a loop whose count may be 0 or negative. Idiom: jle and jng are one instruction. A count of 0x8000 or more is negative here. See also: jg · jcxz · jna

records.heading: jg
records.text: Jump if greater, signed: ZF=0 and SF=OF. Also written jnle. form encoding example bytes jg rel8 7F cb jg $+0x10 7F 0E Flags: none change. Cycles: 1. In a bot: Signed greater: after cmp a, b, jumps if a > b as signed values. Idiom: jg is signed; ja is its unsigned twin. See also: jng · ja · cmp

records.heading: loopne
records.text: Cx -= 1, then jump if cx is not 0 and ZF=0. Also written loopnz. form encoding example bytes loopne rel8 E0 cb loopne $+0x10 E0 0E Flags: none change. Cycles: 1. In a bot: Searches: counts and tests in one instruction, and stops on a match or at the end of the count. Idiom: It does not change the flags, so ZF comes from the instruction before it. After the loop, test ZF to tell a match from the end of the count. See also: loope · loop · repne

records.heading: loope
records.text: Cx -= 1, then jump if cx is not 0 and ZF=1. Also written loopz. form encoding example bytes loope rel8 E1 cb loope $+0x10 E1 0E Flags: none change. Cycles: 1. In a bot: Goes on while a test says equal, up to cx times. Idiom: loopz and loope are one instruction. When cx reaches 0 it stops whatever ZF is. See also: loopne · loop · repe

records.heading: loop
records.text: Cx -= 1, then jump if cx is not 0. form encoding example bytes loop rel8 E2 cb loop $+0x10 E2 0E Flags: none change. Cycles: 1. In a bot: Counts a loop in one instruction: cx -= 1, and jump while cx is not 0. The dwarf counts its lap with it. Idiom: With cx = 0, loop wraps cx to 0xFFFF and runs 65,536 times: guard it with jcxz. The target is rel8: at most 128 bytes back from the end of the loop. See also: jcxz · dec · rep

records.heading: jcxz
records.text: Jump if cx is 0: guards a loop that would run 65,536 times. form encoding example bytes jcxz rel8 E3 cb jcxz $+0x10 E3 0E Flags: none change. Cycles: 1. In a bot: Skips a loop when the count is 0. Idiom: It reads cx, not the flags. There is no jcxnz: use test cx, cx and jnz. A rep needs no guard: with cx = 0 it does nothing. See also: loop · rep

records.heading: string instructions
records.text: Block copies, fills, loads, and scans. Each uses si as the source and di as the destination, and steps them after it runs: by 1 for a byte and 2 for a word, up when DF = 0 and down when DF = 1. DF starts at 0. A prefix repeats an instruction, one iteration a cycle. After each iteration, while cx is not 0 (and, for repe and repne, while ZF says so), ip stays on the prefix, and the process runs the next iteration on its next turn. So rep movsw is not a free 64 KB copy, and an enemy can bomb a copy while it runs. On this page: movsb · movsw · cmpsb · cmpsw · stosb · stosw · lodsb · lodsw · scasb · scasw · cld · std · rep · repe · repne.

records.heading: movsb
records.text: Copy the byte at si to di; step si and di. form encoding example bytes movsb A4 movsb A4 rep movsb F3 A4 rep movsb F3 A4 Flags: none change. Cycles: 1; under a prefix, 1 per iteration. In a bot: Copies one byte and steps si and di. rep movsb copies an odd length exactly. Idiom: movsw copies twice the bytes per cycle; use movsb for an odd tail only. See also: movsw · rep · stosb

records.heading: movsw
records.text: Copy the word at si to di; step si and di. form encoding example bytes movsw A5 movsw A5 rep movsw F3 A5 rep movsw F3 A5 Flags: none change. Cycles: 1; under a prefix, 1 per iteration. In a bot: The imp's instruction and paper's copy. With di one word after si, movsw copies the word it runs to the next word. Idiom: rep movsw takes one cycle per word, and an enemy can bomb the copy before it ends. After it, si and di point past the copy, not at its start. See also: movsb · rep · spl · cld

records.heading: cmpsb
records.text: Compare the byte at si with the byte at di; step si and di. form encoding example bytes cmpsb A6 cmpsb A6 repe cmpsb F3 A6 repe cmpsb F3 A6 repne cmpsb F2 A6 repne cmpsb F2 A6 Cycles: 1; under a prefix, 1 per iteration. In a bot: Compares two runs of bytes: repe cmpsb finds where a copy differs from its source. Idiom: The flags come from [si] - [di]. Both pointers step after the compare, so when it stops they are one past the byte that differs. See also: cmpsw · repe · scasb

records.heading: cmpsw
records.text: Compare the word at si with the word at di; step si and di. form encoding example bytes cmpsw A7 cmpsw A7 repe cmpsw F3 A7 repe cmpsw F3 A7 repne cmpsw F2 A7 repne cmpsw F2 A7 Cycles: 1; under a prefix, 1 per iteration. In a bot: Compares two runs of words: a bot checks its body against a spare copy. Idiom: si and di step by 2, so they stop 2 past the word that differs. See also: cmpsb · repe · repne

records.heading: stosb
records.text: Store al at di; step di. form encoding example bytes stosb AA stosb AA rep stosb F3 AA rep stosb F3 AA Flags: none change. Cycles: 1; under a prefix, 1 per iteration. In a bot: Writes al at di and steps di: bytes of code one at a time, or a fill with rep. Idiom: It steps di down when DF = 1. stosw fills twice as fast. See also: stosw · rep · lodsb

records.heading: stosw
records.text: Store ax at di; step di. form encoding example bytes stosw AB stosw AB rep stosw F3 AB rep stosw F3 AB Flags: none change. Cycles: 1; under a prefix, 1 per iteration. In a bot: The carpet bomb: rep stosw with ax = 0 writes a run of DAT, a word a cycle. Idiom: Point di first: registers start at 0, so a bot that never sets di bombs from address 0 (the linter warns: uninitialized-di). See also: stosb · rep · movsw

records.heading: lodsb
records.text: Load the byte at si into al; step si. form encoding example bytes lodsb AC lodsb AC rep lodsb F3 AC rep lodsb F3 AC Flags: none change. Cycles: 1; under a prefix, 1 per iteration. In a bot: Reads the next byte at si and steps si. Idiom: rep lodsb is legal and useless: each load overwrites al. To find a byte, use repne scasb. See also: lodsw · scasb · stosb

records.heading: lodsw
records.text: Load the word at si into ax; step si. form encoding example bytes lodsw AD lodsw AD rep lodsw F3 AD rep lodsw F3 AD Flags: none change. Cycles: 1; under a prefix, 1 per iteration. In a bot: Reads the next word at si and steps si: a sampler. Idiom: si steps by 2 whatever the data; add to si for a larger stride. See also: lodsb · scasw · loope

records.heading: scasb
records.text: Compare al with the byte at di; step di. form encoding example bytes scasb AE scasb AE repe scasb F3 AE repe scasb F3 AE repne scasb F2 AE repne scasb F2 AE Cycles: 1; under a prefix, 1 per iteration. In a bot: The scanner's search: repe scasb with al = 0 runs over empty core and stops after the first non-zero byte. Idiom: repe goes on while the byte equals al; repne goes on while it does not. Each byte is one cycle, so a scan across a long empty gap is slow. See also: scasw · repe · repne

records.heading: scasw
records.text: Compare ax with the word at di; step di. form encoding example bytes scasw AF scasw AF repe scasw F3 AF repe scasw F3 AF repne scasw F2 AF repne scasw F2 AF Cycles: 1; under a prefix, 1 per iteration. In a bot: Compares ax with a word at di and steps di: a faster scan, 2 bytes a cycle. Idiom: It stops 2 past the word it found. One non-zero byte stops it, in either half. See also: scasb · repe · lodsw

records.heading: cld
records.text: Clear the direction flag: string instructions step up. form encoding example bytes cld FC cld FC Cycles: 1. In a bot: Makes string instructions step up. DF starts at 0, so cld matters after an std. Idiom: A child from spl copies the flags of its parent, DF included. See also: std · movsw · popf

records.heading: std
records.text: Set the direction flag: string instructions step down. form encoding example bytes std FD std FD Cycles: 1. In a bot: Makes string instructions step down: scan or bomb toward lower addresses. Idiom: With DF = 1, a copy starts at the last word: point si and di at the ends of the blocks, not the starts. See also: cld · scasb · stosw

records.heading: rep
records.text: Repeat a string instruction while cx is not 0, cx -= 1 each time, one a cycle. prefix byte takes rep F3 movsb, movsw, stosb, stosw, lodsb, lodsw Flags: the prefix changes none; the string instruction sets its own. Cycles: 1 per iteration. With cx = 0, 1 cycle and no iteration. In a bot: Repeats movs, stos, or lods cx times, one iteration a cycle: the copy and the carpet. Idiom: Between iterations, ip stays on the prefix: a bomb there ends the copy and the process. With cx = 0, it takes one cycle and does nothing. rep and repe are one byte, F3: on cmps and scas, rep repeats while equal. See also: repe · repne · movsw · stosw · loop

records.heading: repe
records.text: Repeat cmps or scas while cx is not 0 and ZF=1 (equal), one a cycle. Also written repz. prefix byte takes repe F3 cmpsb, cmpsw, scasb, scasw Flags: the prefix changes none; the string instruction sets its own. Cycles: 1 per iteration. With cx = 0, 1 cycle and no iteration. In a bot: Repeats cmps or scas while the values are equal: with al = 0, repe scasb passes over empty core. Idiom: It also stops when cx reaches 0. Test ZF after it to tell a hit from the end of the count. See also: rep · repne · scasb · cmpsb

records.heading: repne
records.text: Repeat cmps or scas while cx is not 0 and ZF=0 (not equal), one a cycle. Also written repnz. prefix byte takes repne F2 cmpsb, cmpsw, scasb, scasw Flags: the prefix changes none; the string instruction sets its own. Cycles: 1 per iteration. With cx = 0, 1 cycle and no iteration. In a bot: Repeats cmps or scas while the values differ: finds a given byte or word. Idiom: di stops one past the match (two for scasw). repnz and repne are one prefix. See also: rep · repe · scasb · loopne

records.heading: flag instructions
records.text: Set, clear, or flip CF, and do nothing. DF has its own pair, cld and std, with the string instructions. The flags page says which instruction changes which flag. On this page: clc · stc · cmc · nop.

records.heading: clc
records.text: Clear the carry flag. form encoding example bytes clc F8 clc F8 Cycles: 1. In a bot: Clears CF: before an adc or rcl chain, or as a "no" answer from a subroutine. Idiom: and, or, xor, and test clear CF too. See also: stc · cmc · adc

records.heading: stc
records.text: Set the carry flag. form encoding example bytes stc F9 stc F9 Cycles: 1. In a bot: Sets CF: a "yes" answer from a subroutine, or a 1 to shift in with rcr. Idiom: inc and dec keep CF, so it survives a counter step. See also: clc · cmc · rcr

records.heading: cmc
records.text: Flip the carry flag. form encoding example bytes cmc F5 cmc F5 Cycles: 1. In a bot: Flips CF: turns "below" into "above or equal". Idiom: It flips CF only: ZF still says what the cmp said. See also: clc · stc · jc

records.heading: nop
records.text: Do nothing for a cycle. form encoding example bytes nop 90 nop 90 Flags: none change. Cycles: 1. In a bot: Takes a cycle and does nothing. The imp's movsw is 1 byte; nop fills its word. Idiom: 90 is xchg ax, ax on the 8086; x16c writes xchg ax, ax as 87 C0. A run of 90 bytes is a slide: a process runs through it into whatever comes next. See also: xchg · movsw

records.heading: process control
records.text: The ASM Bots additions (ISA §3.6). On an 8086, 00 is add r/m8, r8, 60..62 are undefined, and F4 and CC stop or trap; here they kill the process or start a new one (see 8086 divergences). A process dies with a reason, which the arena and the debugger show: dat, hlt, and int3 for these instructions, undefined for any other opcode not in the table, and div for a bad divide. On this page: dat · spl · hlt · int3.

records.heading: dat
records.text: Kills the process that runs it: opcode 00, what empty core holds. form encoding example bytes dat imm8 00 ib dat 7 00 07 Flags: none change. Cycles: 1, and the process dies, with reason dat. In a bot: The bomb. A word of two zero bytes is a DAT, and empty core is all DAT. Idiom: Code that falls into dat dies (the linter warns: dat-in-code). resb, resw, and align pad with DAT too. See also: hlt · mov · stosw

records.heading: spl
records.text: Start a new process at the target; this one goes on to the next line. form encoding example bytes spl rel8 60 cb spl $+0x10 60 0E spl rel16 61 cw spl $+0x300 61 FD 02 spl r/m16 62 /0 spl dx 62 C2 Flags: none change. Cycles: 1. In a bot: Starts another process of the bot at the target. The bot still runs one instruction a cycle, shared by its processes: splitting buys survival, not speed. Idiom: At the process cap (64 a bot by default) spl does nothing. spl label is relative; spl dx goes to the absolute address in dx. The child copies all registers, so it starts with the parent's di and bx. See also: jmp · hlt · movsw

records.heading: hlt
records.text: Kill the process that runs it. form encoding example bytes hlt F4 hlt F4 Flags: none change. Cycles: 1, and the process dies, with reason hlt. In a bot: Ends a process on purpose. With fewer processes, each of the rest gets more turns. Idiom: It kills: a bot whose last process runs hlt loses. The linter warns: hlt-in-code. See also: spl · dat · int3

records.heading: int3
records.text: Kill the process that runs it; debugger breakpoints never write it. form encoding example bytes int3 CC int3 CC Flags: none change. Cycles: 1, and the process dies, with reason int3. In a bot: A 1-byte kill. A fill of 0xCC kills a process that runs any byte of it, and a scan for non-zero bytes stops on it: a decoy that bites. Idiom: It kills in the arena and in the debugger alike: the debugger's breakpoints are its own and never write CC. See also: hlt · dat · stosb

records.heading: registers
records.text: Each process has its own registers: eight 16-bit general registers, ip, and FLAGS (ISA §1). ax, bx, cx, and dx each split into two 8-bit halves: al is the low byte of ax, and ah the high byte. There are no segment registers: the core is one flat 64 KB.

records.heading: The registers
records.text: register halves at the start in a bot ax al, ah 0 The accumulator. mul, div, cbw, cwd, lods, stos, and scas use it, and xchg ax, r16 is 1 byte. bx bl, bh 0 A base for addressing ([bx+label]). The base idiom keeps the bot's base address here. cx cl, ch 0 The count. loop, jcxz, and the rep prefixes count it down, and cl is the shift count. dx dl, dh 0 The high half of a mul product and of a div dividend. Free otherwise. si 0 The source of movs, lods, and cmps, and an index for addressing. di 0 The destination of movs, stos, scas, and cmps, and an index for addressing. bp 0 The other base for addressing ([bp+si], [bp+4]). sp the base The stack pointer. push, pop, call, and ret move it. ip the base The address of the next instruction. No instruction names it: jumps, calls, ret, and loop change it, and a rep holds it on the prefix. FLAGS 0x0002 The status flags and DF: see flags. A bot starts with one process, at its base: ip and sp hold the base address, FLAGS holds 0x0002 (bit 1 always reads 1), and the rest hold 0. The stack grows down from the base, into the core under the bot.

records.heading: A new process
records.text: A process that spl starts gets a copy of every register and flag of its parent at that moment, with ip at the target. The two share the core, and nothing else: a later change to a register of one does not reach the other.

records.heading: Registers in addresses
records.text: Only bx and bp (the base) and si and di (the index) can be part of a memory operand: [bx+si+4], [bp+di], [di-2]. See ModR/M addressing.

records.heading: Register codes
records.text: The 3-bit code of each register, in the ModR/M reg and r/m fields and in the low bits of a +r opcode. An instruction on bytes reads the code as an 8-bit register, so code 4 is sp in a word instruction and ah in a byte one. code bits 16-bit 8-bit 0 000 ax al 1 001 cx cl 2 010 dx dl 3 011 bx bl 4 100 sp ah 5 101 bp ch 6 110 si dh 7 111 di bh

records.heading: flags
records.text: FLAGS is a 16-bit register of each process. x16c uses seven of its bits: six status flags, which instructions set from their results, and DF, which steers the string instructions. Bit 1 always reads 1, and every other bit reads 0, the I and T of the 8086 included. The debugger shows them in the 8086 order:

records.heading: The flags
records.text: flag bit name is 1 when read by CF 0 carry an add carries out of the top bit, a subtract borrows, or a shift pushes a 1 out jc, jnc, ja, jna, adc, sbb, rcl, rcr PF 2 parity the low byte of the result has an even count of 1 bits jpe, jpo AF 4 auxiliary carry a carry or borrow crosses bit 3 (for decimal math, which x16c leaves out) lahf, pushf ZF 6 zero the result is 0 jz, jnz, ja, jna, jg, jng, loope, loopne, repe, repne SF 7 sign bit 15 of the result (bit 7 of a byte) is 1 js, jns, jl, jnl, jg, jng DF 10 direction std sets it and cld clears it every string instruction: it steps si and di down when DF = 1 OF 11 overflow a signed result does not fit jo, jno, jl, jnl, jg, jng

records.heading: What changes each flag
records.text: Each instruction page shows its flags row. This is the same, flag by flag: "from the result" is set or cleared by what the instruction computed. An instruction not listed never changes the flag. flag from the result set to 0 set to 1 CF popf, sahf, add, adc, sub, sbb, cmp, neg, cmpsb, cmpsw, scasb, scasw, mul, imul, shl, shr, sar, rol, ror, rcl, rcr, cmc and, or, xor, test, clc stc PF popf, sahf, add, adc, sub, sbb, cmp, neg, cmpsb, cmpsw, scasb, scasw, inc, dec, and, or, xor, test, shl, shr, sar mul, imul AF popf, sahf, add, adc, sub, sbb, cmp, neg, cmpsb, cmpsw, scasb, scasw, inc, dec, shl mul, imul, and, or, xor, test, shr, sar ZF popf, sahf, add, adc, sub, sbb, cmp, neg, cmpsb, cmpsw, scasb, scasw, inc, dec, and, or, xor, test, shl, shr, sar mul, imul SF popf, sahf, add, adc, sub, sbb, cmp, neg, cmpsb, cmpsw, scasb, scasw, inc, dec, and, or, xor, test, shl, sar mul, imul, shr DF popf cld std OF popf, add, adc, sub, sbb, cmp, neg, cmpsb, cmpsw, scasb, scasw, mul, imul, inc, dec, shl, shr, rol, ror, rcl, rcr and, or, xor, test, sar Where the 8086 leaves a flag undefined, x16c gives it a fixed value, the one the silicon gives: and, or, xor, and test clear AF; mul and imul clear SF, ZF, AF, and PF; div and idiv change no flag. A shift or rotate by a count of 0 changes no flag.

records.heading: Saving and loading
records.text: pushf and popf save and load all of FLAGS through the stack. lahf and sahf copy SF, ZF, AF, PF, and CF to and from ah. A child of spl starts with its parent's flags, DF included.

records.heading: Conditions
records.text: The conditional jumps read the flags: control flow has the table of what each one tests.

records.heading: The core
records.text: The core is 65,536 bytes, addresses 0x0000 to 0xFFFF: one flat address space, shared by every bot, with no segments. Every address wraps: one past 0xFFFF is 0x0000. A word is 2 bytes, low byte first, and a word at 0xFFFF takes its high byte from 0x0000.

records.heading: Empty core is DAT
records.text: The core starts as zeros, and 00 is dat. A process that runs into empty core dies, and so does one that walks off the end of its code. A bomb is 2 zero bytes: mov word [di], 0.

records.heading: Ownership
records.text: Beside the core is an ownership map: one byte per address, which bot wrote it last. Loading a bot counts as its write. The arena colors the core by it. It has no effect on the battle: any process can read or write any address.

records.heading: Placement
records.text: A bot is at most 512 bytes. The loader puts each bot at a base address drawn from the battle's seed, at least 1,024 bytes from every other bot, wrapping included, and does not move or relocate it. The same seed and the same bots give the same places, so every battle can be run again. Each bot starts with one process at its base, and may have up to 64 (the process cap). A battle ends when one bot or none is alive, or at 100,000 cycles (80,000 on the hills).

records.heading: The stack
records.text: sp starts at the base, so a push or call writes the word just under the bot, and the stack grows down into the core. That core belongs to nobody: an enemy bomb there changes what pop and ret read.

records.heading: Position independence
records.text: A label is an offset from the start of the bot, the address it would have at org 0. So [label] is an absolute address, [disp16]: the place label in the core, not the bot's copy of it. To reach its own data, a bot finds its base and adds the label to it: call pushes the address of .here, pop takes it, and sub takes away the offset of .here, which leaves the base. From then on, [bx+label] is the bot's own label. The linter warns on a memory operand with no register, absolute-address. Jumps, calls, loop, and spl label are relative, and need no base.

records.heading: modr/m addressing
records.text: A memory operand is a base register (bx or bp), an index register (si or di), and a constant displacement, each one optional, in any order: [bx+si+4], [4+si], [di], [bx+label], [0x0100] (ISA §2.2, §6.3). The byte after the opcode, ModR/M, says which of them an instruction uses. mod picks memory or a register and the displacement size; reg is a register or an opcode extension; r/m picks the address.

records.heading: The fields
records.text: mod means 00 memory, no displacement; with r/m 110, [disp16] 01 memory, plus a signed disp8 (-128..127) 10 memory, plus a disp16 11 a register: r/m is a register code reg holds the other operand's register code, or, in a group opcode such as 80 or F7, an extension that picks the instruction: /0 is add and /5 is sub under 83.

records.heading: The 8 forms
records.text: Each r/m code with each mod, as mov dx, … (reg = 010, dx) assembles them: r/m address mod 00 mod 01: + disp8 mod 10: + disp16 000 [bx+si] mov dx, [bx+si] · 8B 10 mov dx, [bx+si+4] · 8B 50 04 mov dx, [bx+si+0x1234] · 8B 90 34 12 001 [bx+di] mov dx, [bx+di] · 8B 11 mov dx, [bx+di+4] · 8B 51 04 mov dx, [bx+di+0x1234] · 8B 91 34 12 010 [bp+si] mov dx, [bp+si] · 8B 12 mov dx, [bp+si+4] · 8B 52 04 mov dx, [bp+si+0x1234] · 8B 92 34 12 011 [bp+di] mov dx, [bp+di] · 8B 13 mov dx, [bp+di+4] · 8B 53 04 mov dx, [bp+di+0x1234] · 8B 93 34 12 100 [si] mov dx, [si] · 8B 14 mov dx, [si+4] · 8B 54 04 mov dx, [si+0x1234] · 8B 94 34 12 101 [di] mov dx, [di] · 8B 15 mov dx, [di+4] · 8B 55 04 mov dx, [di+0x1234] · 8B 95 34 12 110 [bp] mov dx, [0x1234] · 8B 16 34 12: [disp16], absolute mov dx, [bp+4] · 8B 56 04 mov dx, [bp+0x1234] · 8B 96 34 12 111 [bx] mov dx, [bx] · 8B 17 mov dx, [bx+4] · 8B 57 04 mov dx, [bx+0x1234] · 8B 97 34 12 [bp] alone has no mod 00 form: that slot is [disp16]. The assembler writes it as mod 01 with a disp8 of 0, one byte longer than [bx].

records.heading: One instruction, byte by byte
records.text: byte is means C7 opcode mov r/m16, imm16, with ModR/M 40 ModR/M 01 000 000 mod 01: a disp8 follows; reg /0: mov; r/m 000: [bx+si] 04 disp8 +4 41 00 imm16 0x0041, low byte first So mov word [bx+si+4], 0x41 is C7 40 04 41 00: 5 bytes.

records.heading: Rules
records.text: There is no [bx+bp] and no [si+di]: one base and one index at most. Such an operand is the error invalid-address. A displacement of -128..127 takes a disp8, and any other a disp16. A label is a number like any other, so [bx+label] near the start of a bot is short. [label] and [0x0100] are absolute: the linter warns with absolute-address (see memory model). When no operand is a register, the size must be said: mov word [bx], 0, not mov [bx], 0 (size-not-specified). lea computes the address and reads nothing: lea di, [bx+end] is di = bx + end.

records.heading: directives
records.text: The source is NASM syntax for the 16-bit 8086, bits 16 implied (ISA §6). Mnemonics, registers, and directives take any case; labels are case-sensitive. A ; starts a comment to the end of the line.

records.heading: Metadata
records.text: directive does %name "Dwarf" The name the arena and the hills show. Required, once. %author "A. K. Dewdney" Who wrote it. %strategy "Bomb every 4th byte" One line on the tactic. The linter warns without it (no-strategy). %version "1.2" Any text.

records.heading: Data and space
records.text: directive does db 1, 2, "ab", 0 Bytes.
